items.stem: Explain Myrdal’s theory of cumulative causation.
items.answer: A region gains an initial advantage (resources, port, capital); new industry creates jobs and income; the multiplier attracts more firms, services and workers; tax revenue improves infrastructure; growth becomes self-reinforcing while the periphery suffers backwash.

items.stem: Explain why regional disparities develop within countries.
items.answer: Physical factors (resources, climate, relief, coasts); historical advantages (colonial ports, capital cities); infrastructure and investment concentrated in core; agglomeration; migration of skilled people; government policy.

items.stem: Nadia argues that regional disparities within countries are inevitable. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to cumulative causation, policy and infrastructure.
items.answer: For: Cumulative causation and agglomeration concentrate growth in core regions; physical advantages persist; disparities are found in almost all countries. Against: Spread effects, regional policy, infrastructure and decentralisation can narrow gaps (Friedmann’s stage 4; EU cohesion funds; China’s western development); some peripheries have grown fast. Conclusion: Disparities arise naturally, but their size can be reduced by policy and spread effects.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “core region”?
options: Negative effects of core growth on the periphery, such as out-migration of young skilled workers and capital.
A less developed area with lower incomes and out-migration, dependent on the core.
Myrdal’s (1957) idea that once a region gains an advantage, the multiplier effect attracts further growth, widening disparities.
A prosperous area with concentrated wealth, investment, population and decision-making.

items.stem: Explain the strategies used to reduce regional disparities.
items.answer: Infrastructure (roads, railways, broadband); grants and tax incentives for firms; growth poles and SEZs; relocating government offices; education and training; EU structural funds; controls on growth in the core.

items.stem: Explain why regional policies often have limited success.
items.answer: Incentives attract capital-intensive firms with few jobs ("cathedrals in the desert" in southern Italy); corruption; firms leave when grants end; peripheral regions lack skills; core growth continues.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that top-down regional policies have failed to reduce regional disparities?
items.answer: For: Southern Italy remains far poorer despite decades of investment; Brazil’s north-east lags; China’s coastal-inland gap persists. Against: Some policies helped: EU funds in Poland and Ireland, China’s western provinces grew faster than the east after 2000; Brasília and Manaus created new growth centres. Conclusion: Results are mixed: policies can raise growth in peripheral regions, but closing gaps fully needs sustained investment, skills and local initiative.

items.stem: Explain the impacts of China’s Western Development Strategy.
items.answer: Huge investment in roads, railways, airports and energy (West-East gas pipeline, Qinghai-Tibet railway); faster growth in western provinces after 2000; cities such as Chengdu and Chongqing boomed; but environmental damage, ethnic tensions and gaps in incomes remain.

items.stem: Briefly describe the strategies used to promote regional development, for Italy (the Mezzogiorno) or another example of regional development within a country.
items.answer: Italy (the Mezzogiorno): Cassa per il Mezzogiorno (1950-84): land reform, roads, irrigation and large state industrial plants (Taranto steelworks, petrochemicals in Sicily and Sardinia); later EU structural and cohesion funds; motorways such as the A2 to Reggio Calabria.

items.stem: Briefly describe the strategies used to promote regional development, for Brazil (the North and North-east) or another example of regional development within a country.
items.answer: Brazil (the North and North-east): SUDENE (1959) for the north-east; Brasília (1960) and roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway; Manaus Free Trade Zone (1967) with tax incentives for electronics and motorcycle assembly; Bolsa Família cash transfers from 2003.

items.stem: Using a named example of regional development within a country you have studied, evaluate the extent to which regional disparities have been reduced.
items.answer: Model answer (China (Western Development Strategy)): From 2000: investment in infrastructure (Qinghai-Tibet railway 2006, highways, airports), West-East gas pipeline and electricity transmission, Chongqing and Chengdu as growth poles, tax incentives, ecological programmes such as Grain for Green. Western provinces grew faster than the coast in parts of the 2000s and 2010s and inland cities attracted manufacturing; but the absolute gap remains large, much investment is state-led and capital-intensive, and environmental and ethnic tensions have increased.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how spread effects can reduce regional disparities. (b) A student writes: “Regional disparities always narrow over time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Core growth raises demand for food and raw materials from the periphery; firms relocate to cheaper land and labour; investment and innovation diffuse; remittances. (b) Not correct. Cumulative causation can widen them without intervention.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how spread effects can reduce regional disparities. (b) A revision website states: “Backwash effects benefit the periphery.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Core growth raises demand for food and raw materials from the periphery; firms relocate to cheaper land and labour; investment and innovation diffuse; remittances. (b) Not correct. They take workers and capital away from the periphery.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Capital cities are often core regions.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why regional disparities develop within countries.
items.answer: (a) Correct. They concentrate government, finance and investment. (b) Physical factors (resources, climate, relief, coasts); historical advantages (colonial ports, capital cities); infrastructure and investment concentrated in core; agglomeration; migration of skilled people; government policy.

items.stem: Table 28.1 shows GDP per capita (thousand US$, PPP) by region in a country similar to Thailand: Bangkok region 21.7, Central 20.3, East 11, North 9.5, North-east 7.4. (a) Suggest why the CV is a better measure of regional disparity than the ratio of richest to poorest. (b) Suggest limitations of using GDP per capita to measure regional disparities.
items.answer: (a) It uses all regions rather than only the extremes and is independent of the units, allowing comparison between countries and over time. (b) It ignores inequality within regions, the cost of living, the informal economy and other aspects of well-being such as health and education.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that regional disparities within countries are inevitable? In your answer you may refer to cumulative causation, policy and migration.
items.answer: For: Cumulative causation and agglomeration concentrate growth in core regions; physical advantages persist; disparities are found in almost all countries. Against: Spread effects, regional policy, infrastructure and decentralisation can narrow gaps (Friedmann’s stage 4; EU cohesion funds; China’s western development); some peripheries have grown fast. Conclusion: Disparities arise naturally, but their size can be reduced by policy and spread effects.

items.stem: Table 28.1 shows GDP per capita (thousand US$, PPP) by region in a country similar to China: East coast 27.6, North-east 10.6, Central 10, West 7.9. (a) Explain how the theory of cumulative causation could account for these disparities. (b) Suggest why the CV is a better measure of regional disparity than the ratio of richest to poorest.
items.answer: (a) The East coast region gained an early advantage (port, capital, resources); investment and the multiplier attracted more firms and skilled migrants, while backwash effects drained workers and capital from the West region. (b) It uses all regions rather than only the extremes and is independent of the units, allowing comparison between countries and over time.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the growth pole concept. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Infrastructure investment can reduce the isolation of peripheral regions.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Concentrating investment in a key industry or city creates linkages and multiplier effects that spread growth to surrounding areas over time. (b) Correct. Roads, railways and broadband reduce costs and improve access.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why regional policies often have limited success. (b) Explain the growth pole concept.
items.answer: (a) Incentives attract capital-intensive firms with few jobs ("cathedrals in the desert" in southern Italy); corruption; firms leave when grants end; peripheral regions lack skills; core growth continues. (b) Concentrating investment in a key industry or city creates linkages and multiplier effects that spread growth to surrounding areas over time.

Explain why the absolute gap can widen even when the relative gap narrows.
items.answer: The core starts from a much higher base, so a smaller percentage growth still adds more dollars than faster growth in the periphery.

items.stem: “Top-down regional policies have failed to reduce regional disparities.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Southern Italy remains far poorer despite decades of investment; Brazil’s north-east lags; China’s coastal-inland gap persists. Against: Some policies helped: EU funds in Poland and Ireland, China’s western provinces grew faster than the east after 2000; Brasília and Manaus created new growth centres. Conclusion: Results are mixed: policies can raise growth in peripheral regions, but closing gaps fully needs sustained investment, skills and local initiative.

items.stem: Briefly evaluate the success of these strategies, for Italy (the Mezzogiorno) or another example of regional development within a country.
items.answer: Italy (the Mezzogiorno): Infrastructure and living standards improved, but GDP per capita remains about half to 60% of the north; plants created few linked jobs ("cathedrals in the desert"); corruption and organised crime diverted funds; out-migration continues.

items.stem: Kwame argues that regional disparities are best reduced by investment in infrastructure. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Roads, railways, energy and broadband reduce isolation and costs (China’s western railways, EU-funded motorways); attract firms and tourism. Against: Infrastructure alone can increase backwash by making it easier to serve the periphery from the core; education, health, local enterprise, governance and cash transfers (Bolsa Família) may be more effective. Conclusion: Infrastructure is necessary but not sufficient; it must be combined with investment in people and institutions.
